query: (Cathay MD) Build a model to organise/optimise routes and service so Overall Rating > 7.

per_column.name: Haul_Type
per_column.rationale: Categorising each Route into Long-haul vs Short/Medium-haul is a clean, genuinely new grouping axis directly relevant to a route-optimisation model. Values are soundly derivable from the Route field: Manchester-Sydney and HK-Melbourne read as Long-haul, HK-Tokyo/Manila-HK/Beijing-Bangkok as Short/Medium-haul. Well grounded.

per_column.name: Composite_Service_Score
per_column.rationale: A single aggregate of the several 1-5 service-rating columns gives a usable modelling target/feature, though it partly overlaps the underlying dimension columns. The fractional values are consistent with averaging existing numeric rating columns, so values are derivable from the table.

per_column.name: Value_Gap
per_column.rationale: A gap between Value-For-Money and service quality is a legitimate new axis for a pricing/value lens on the optimisation query. Computed from existing rating columns so it is grounded; the exact sign convention is a little opaque but nothing is invented beyond present columns.

per_column.name: Route_Performance_Tier
per_column.rationale: Route-level Low/Medium/High tiering is highly pertinent to organising/optimising routes. Values appear consistent with aggregating ratings by route (very negative Manchester-Sydney = Low, praise-heavy Manila-HK = High); one positive HK-Melbourne review lands as Medium, plausible for a route-level average. Grounded in existing numeric data.

per_column.name: Weakest_Dimension
per_column.rationale: Identifying the lowest-scoring service dimension per row is exactly the kind of targeting signal the improvement query needs. Mostly a sound reading of the numeric rating columns; a couple of rows (e.g. a review whose only complaint is legroom labelled 'Value For Money') diverge from the review text, but the value is still derivable from the numeric ratings present, so not a hallucination.

per_column.name: Improvement_Priority
per_column.rationale: Actionable, but largely a relabelling of Weakest_Dimension into an action verb (VFM->Price/Value Reset, Seat->Seat/Comfort Upgrade), so it adds limited independent leverage; the label set is also internally redundant (Enhancement vs Uplift vs Improvement variants). Values follow deterministically from the weakest dimension, hence grounded.

per_column.name: High_Rating_Potential
per_column.rationale: Directly tied to the Overall Rating > 7 goal, but as a bare Yes/No it is coarse and risks near-restating Overall Rating. The samples are also hard to reconcile (a strongly positive 'best cabin crew' review = No, while a mixed part-poor review = Yes), suggesting an opaque heuristic; still derived from present ratings rather than invented facts, so no outright hallucination.

judge.rationale: The set gives several real analytical axes for the route/service optimisation query: Haul_Type, Route_Performance_Tier and Weakest_Dimension provide new grouping/targeting leverage, while Composite_Service_Score and Value_Gap add modelling features. Improvement_Priority is mostly a restatement of Weakest_Dimension and High_Rating_Potential is a coarse, somewhat opaque binary, dragging holistic usefulness down slightly. Groundedness is generally solid: every column is derivable from the Route field or the existing 1-5 rating columns, and the evidence rows show plausible readings; minor row-level divergences from review prose and the inconsistent High_Rating_Potential logic keep it short of excellent, but no invented source facts are observed.
